title: MySQL indexes
context: How do MySQL indexes work, and when do they stop being used?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): MySQL questions
source.note: Translated and condensed into English; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: InnoDB indexes are B+ trees. Leaves hold rows in the clustered (primary key) index, or primary keys in secondary indexes. A secondary lookup needs a second lookup in the clustered index, unless the index covers the query. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: an index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a, on a and b, or on all three, but not on b alone. Functions on the column, leading wildcards in LIKE, and implicit type conversion usually stop an index from being used. Check with EXPLAIN.

points.title: B+ tree and clustered index
points.why: The primary key tree holds the rows, so the key choice affects every index.

points.title: Leftmost prefix
points.why: A composite index only helps queries that use its first columns.

points.title: Covering index
points.why: If the index holds all columns the query needs, MySQL skips the row lookup.
